claims.heading: ## Summary
claims.claim: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC ✅[^rfc9114]
claims.context: **TL;DR:** HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and because TCP's loss recovery cannot see that multiplexing, a lost or reordered packet stalls every active transaction, including those the lost packet did not directly affect ✅[^rfc9114]. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC ✅[^rfc9114], where a lost packet blocks only the streams that had data in it ✅[^rfc9000]. Head-of-line (HOL) blocking does not disappear in HTTP/3: it remains inside a single stream, in packets that carry several streams, in QPACK header compression when the decoder allows it, and in the congestion controller the whole connection shares (§6.1).

claims.context: - **Transport layer (TCP).** HTTP/2 addresses this by allowing messages to be interleaved on the same connection, but RFC 9113 also notes that "TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol" ✅[^rfc9113]. TCP's loss recovery cannot see HTTP/2's parallel streams, so a lost or reordered packet stalls all active transactions, whether or not the lost packet carried their data ✅[^rfc9114]. §6.2 explains an overview sentence of RFC 9113 that seems to say otherwise.

claims.heading: ## 1. Mental model
claims.claim: QUIC has no way to order bytes on different streams ✅[^rfc9000]
claims.context: HTTP/3 hands multiplexing to QUIC, which provides reliability per stream and congestion control across the entire connection ✅[^rfc9114]. QUIC has no way to order bytes on different streams ✅[^rfc9000], so the in-order rule behind TCP HOL blocking now applies to one stream at a time. Four kinds of blocking remain, all listed in §6.1: a gap inside one stream, a lost packet that carried several streams, QPACK blocked streams, and one congestion controller for the whole connection.

claims.heading: ## 2. Concept architecture
claims.claim: Many can be open at once, and either endpoint interleaves their frames ✅[^rfc9113]
claims.context: | Stream | An independent, bidirectional sequence of frames inside one HTTP/2 connection. Many can be open at once, and either endpoint interleaves their frames ✅[^rfc9113] | A unidirectional or bidirectional channel of ordered bytes inside a QUIC connection, which can carry many streams at the same time ✅[^rfc9000] |

claims.heading: ## 2. Concept architecture
claims.claim: RFC 9114 sums it up: HTTP/2 "provides an absolute ordering between frames across all streams, while QUIC provides this guarantee on each stream only" ✅[^rfc9114]
claims.context: | Where order is guaranteed | Across all frames of all streams | Within each stream only. RFC 9114 sums it up: HTTP/2 "provides an absolute ordering between frames across all streams, while QUIC provides this guarantee on each stream only" ✅[^rfc9114] |

claims.heading: ## 2. Concept architecture
claims.claim: It starts empty, and the encoder fills it with instructions sent on the encoder stream ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: | Header compression | HPACK (RFC 7541): each endpoint has one encoder context and one decoder context for all field blocks on the connection, and the dynamic table is each context's main state ✅[^rfc9113] | QPACK (RFC 9204; "a name, not an abbreviation"): a dynamic table, a first-in, first-out list of field lines that encoder and decoder share. It starts empty, and the encoder fills it with instructions sent on the encoder stream ✅[^rfc9204] |

claims.heading: ## 2. Concept architecture
claims.claim: Limit-based, at two levels: stream flow control and connection flow control ✅[^rfc9000]
claims.context: | Flow control | Credit-based: with WINDOW_UPDATE frames, receivers advertise how many octets they will accept on a stream and on the whole connection ✅[^rfc9113] | Limit-based, at two levels: stream flow control and connection flow control ✅[^rfc9000] |

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: TCP's in-order guarantee means that after a packet loss, all the data that follows the loss on the connection must wait for the loss to be repaired before HTTP can see it ✅[^fastly]
claims.context: 1. HTTP/2 interleaves frames of many streams into one TCP byte stream (§2). TCP's in-order guarantee means that after a packet loss, all the data that follows the loss on the connection must wait for the loss to be repaired before HTTP can see it ✅[^fastly].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: HTTP/2 framing relies on that order too: recipients process frames in the order they are received, and the order of HEADERS and DATA frames is semantically significant ✅[^rfc9113]
claims.context: 2. HTTP/2 framing relies on that order too: recipients process frames in the order they are received, and the order of HEADERS and DATA frames is semantically significant ✅[^rfc9113].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: Encoded field sections must arrive and be decoded in the order they were encoded, which keeps the dynamic state of both endpoints in sync ✅[^rfc9114]
claims.context: 3. HPACK adds a second dependence on order. Encoded field sections must arrive and be decoded in the order they were encoded, which keeps the dynamic state of both endpoints in sync ✅[^rfc9114]. §5.1 lists the MUST rules RFC 9113 sets on field blocks.

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: The receiver uses each STREAM frame's Stream ID and Offset fields to put the data in order ✅[^rfc9000]
claims.context: 1. QUIC multiplexes by interleaving STREAM frames from several streams into QUIC packets, and one packet can carry STREAM frames from one or more streams. The receiver uses each STREAM frame's Stream ID and Offset fields to put the data in order ✅[^rfc9000], buffering out-of-order data up to the flow-control limit it advertised (§5.2).

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: Frames that carry encoded fields only reference the table's state at a given time ✅[^rfc9114]
claims.context: 2. QPACK instead makes every change to the dynamic table on a single unidirectional stream, which keeps those updates in a total order. Frames that carry encoded fields only reference the table's state at a given time ✅[^rfc9114].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: A reference to the dynamic table risks it while the encoder has no acknowledgment that the entry is available at the decoder ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: 3. References to the static table and literal representations never risk HOL blocking. A reference to the dynamic table risks it while the encoder has no acknowledgment that the entry is available at the decoder ✅[^rfc9204].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: Referencing only acknowledged entries avoids blocking but may mean literals, and the larger field sections can leave the encoder blocked on congestion or flow-control limits ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: 7. The encoder chooses its risk. If SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS permits it, referencing entries still in transit can often improve compression, but on loss or reordering the stream can become blocked at the decoder. Referencing only acknowledged entries avoids blocking but may mean literals, and the larger field sections can leave the encoder blocked on congestion or flow-control limits ✅[^rfc9204].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: If an endpoint cannot make sure its peer always has more flow-control credit than the peer's bandwidth-delay product (BDP: bandwidth times round-trip time) on the connection, flow control limits its receive throughput, and packet loss can leave gaps in the receive buffer that keep the application from consuming data and freeing buffer space ✅[^rfc9000]
claims.context: 2. If an endpoint cannot make sure its peer always has more flow-control credit than the peer's bandwidth-delay product (BDP: bandwidth times round-trip time) on the connection, flow control limits its receive throughput, and packet loss can leave gaps in the receive buffer that keep the application from consuming data and freeing buffer space ✅[^rfc9000].

claims.heading: ## 3. How it works
claims.claim: One loss slows HTTP/2's single connection, while HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections slows only the one that lost a packet, and in QUIC a loss on any stream slows every stream of the connection ✅[^marx]
claims.context: Congestion control works per TCP or QUIC connection, not per stream. One loss slows HTTP/2's single connection, while HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections slows only the one that lost a packet, and in QUIC a loss on any stream slows every stream of the connection ✅[^marx].

claims.heading: ## 4. Worked examples
claims.claim: Over TCP, when packet 2 is lost, TCP keeps packet 3 in its receive buffer until the retransmitted copy of packet 2 arrives, at least one round trip later, so both streams wait although stream 1's DATA frame in packet 3 was usable ✅[^marx]
claims.context: The setup, from one practitioner's figures: a JavaScript file on stream 1 and a CSS file on stream 2, sent in three packets. Packet 2 carries only stream 2 data and packet 3 carries data for both streams. Over TCP, when packet 2 is lost, TCP keeps packet 3 in its receive buffer until the retransmitted copy of packet 2 arrives, at least one round trip later, so both streams wait although stream 1's DATA frame in packet 3 was usable ✅[^marx].

claims.heading: ## 4. Worked examples

claims.heading: ## 4. Worked examples
claims.claim: When the losses are spread over both streams, both are HOL blocked, each because it still has to be put in order by itself ✅[^marx]
claims.context: The same author models one burst of 8 lost packets while 2 streams download. When the streams are sent one after the other, QUIC's HOL removal barely helps, because the packets received after the loss belong to the stream that lost data. When they are multiplexed and, by chance, all 8 losses hit one stream, the other stream can be processed. When the losses are spread over both streams, both are HOL blocked, each because it still has to be put in order by itself ✅[^marx].

claims.heading: ## 5. Reference & invariants
claims.claim: Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream ✅[^rfc9113]
claims.context: | Field block framing | Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream ✅[^rfc9113] |

claims.heading: ## 5. Reference & invariants
claims.claim: A receiver MUST treat any other frame type, or a frame on a different stream, as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR ✅[^rfc9113]
claims.context: | CONTINUATION | A HEADERS frame without the END_HEADERS flag set MUST be followed by a CONTINUATION frame for the same stream. A receiver MUST treat any other frame type, or a frame on a different stream, as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR ✅[^rfc9113] |

claims.heading: ## 5. Reference & invariants
claims.claim: SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE adjusts the value for new streams; the connection window can only be changed with WINDOW_UPDATE frames ✅[^rfc9113]

claims.heading: ## 5. Reference & invariants
claims.claim: Since a blocked sender is not required to send them, a receiver MUST NOT wait for those frames before sending MAX_STREAM_DATA or MAX_DATA ✅[^rfc9000]

claims.heading: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
claims.claim: - Cloudflare (2020, Rank 4): uploading a 10MB object over a network with 200Mbps of bandwidth and a 40ms RTT, with Cloudflare's production configuration, HTTP/2 measured almost half the speed of HTTP/1.1, while at 5Mbps upload and 20ms RTT the two were almost identical ✅[^cfupload]
claims.context: - Cloudflare (2020, Rank 4): uploading a 10MB object over a network with 200Mbps of bandwidth and a 40ms RTT, with Cloudflare's production configuration, HTTP/2 measured almost half the speed of HTTP/1.1, while at 5Mbps upload and 20ms RTT the two were almost identical ✅[^cfupload]. The bottleneck was HTTP/2 flow control: the application layer runs its own receiver flow control, and NGINX uses a fixed-size receive buffer, which limits upload speed when the link's BDP is larger than the request body buffer ✅[^cfupload].

claims.heading: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
claims.claim: For an HTTP/2 server to switch quickly to a high-priority response, H2O says the TCP send buffer should hold only the packets in flight, and TLS records must be small enough to avoid HOL blocking; the cost is more CPU (processor) cycles and slightly higher latency ✅[^h2o]
claims.context: HOL blocking can also start on the sending side. For an HTTP/2 server to switch quickly to a high-priority response, H2O says the TCP send buffer should hold only the packets in flight, and TLS records must be small enough to avoid HOL blocking; the cost is more CPU (processor) cycles and slightly higher latency ✅[^h2o]. H2O's knobs for this are in §5.4.

claims.claim: (WWW 2024, Rank 2): over fast Internet, the UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 stack showed a data rate up to 45.2% lower than TCP+TLS+HTTP/2, and the gap grew with bandwidth; on Chrome, QUIC fell behind above about 500 Mbps and was 45.2% slower than HTTP/2 at 1 Gbps ✅[^zhang]

claims.claim: The kernel's UDP stack reads many more packets than TCP's because none of the QUIC implementations they examined uses UDP generic receive offload (GRO) ✅[^zhang]
claims.context: - The cause, per Zhang et al.: high receiver-side processing overhead, in particular excessive data packets and QUIC's user-space ACKs (acknowledgments). The kernel's UDP stack reads many more packets than TCP's because none of the QUIC implementations they examined uses UDP generic receive offload (GRO) ✅[^zhang].

claims.heading: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions
claims.claim: Partly resolved conflict on QUIC's CPU cost: Robin Marx (2020, Rank 4) names per-packet encryption, which needs more CPU than encrypting larger blocks, as one of the main reasons QUIC can still be slower than TCP in current implementations ✅[^marx]
claims.context: Partly resolved conflict on QUIC's CPU cost: Robin Marx (2020, Rank 4) names per-packet encryption, which needs more CPU than encrypting larger blocks, as one of the main reasons QUIC can still be slower than TCP in current implementations ✅[^marx]. Zhang et al. (Rank 2) govern the measured main cause, receiver-side processing (excessive data packets and user-space ACKs, with no UDP GRO, as above), and found that the cipher suite made no significant difference: both their stacks used the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher, and benchmarking other cipher suites did not significantly change the results ✅[^zhang]. The cost of per-packet against per-record encryption that Marx raises is still untested, since their test varied cipher suites, not that.

claims.claim: On the 1% to 5% of networks where QUIC packets over UDP are blocked or limited, HTTP/2's natural fallback to TLS over TCP can be used ✅[^edeline]
